Every point of Quality Score in Google Ads is a discount on what you pay per click.

Static ads are great for testing. You can throw ten variations up in a day and see which headline or image gets a click. But each one can only carry one idea. A stat, a claim, a single visual hook.

Video is different. You get thirty seconds to walk someone from "I've never heard of this" to "I get why I need this." Problem, solution, proof, all in one asset.

The best-performing accounts I've seen don't choose one over the other. They run static for fast, cheap signal on what resonates, then build video around whichever idea wins.

Your free users are not going to upgrade themselves.

Free tier signups feel like a win, but the upgrade doesn't happen on its own. You have to go get it.

Start with the basics. Email nurtures that walk them through the features they haven't touched yet. In-app tooltips that show up right when they hit a paywall moment.

Then go further. Invite your best free users to a webinar built around the exact use case your paid plan unlocks. Reach out directly on LinkedIn to the ones showing real usage. Offer a limited-time discount to nudge the fence-sitters.

None of this is complicated. It just requires someone to own it instead of assuming the product will sell itself.

Stop reshooting your whole ad every time you want to test something new.

Here's the shortcut nobody tells you about creative testing. Film your core ad once. The offer, the proof, the CTA, all of it.

Then before you wrap the shoot, grab five or six different hooks. Different angles, different first lines, different scroll-stops.

Mix and match those hooks against the same core ad in your ad platform. The hook is what decides whether someone stops scrolling. Everything else barely matters if the first three seconds don't land.

Once you see which hook wins, you're not just done testing. You've got direction for your next shoot too.

One session. One core asset. A dozen ways to learn what actually grabs attention.

posts.content:
Your funnel isn't broken everywhere. It's broken in exactly one place, and most teams never find it.

Most marketers respond to a slow quarter by pushing more top of funnel. More ads, more content, more volume.

That's the expensive fix. The cheap fix is bottleneck analysis.

List out every step between a stranger and a closed deal. Signup, attendee, lead, meeting request, opportunity, close.

Now track two numbers between each step. Conversion rate and cost per action. Cost per signup is easy. Cost per meeting request is the one that actually matters.

One step will look worse than the rest. That's your bottleneck, and it's usually not where you assumed.

Fix that one step before you add a single dollar of new spend. A funnel with one broken link backs up everywhere behind it.

Where does your funnel actually leak, top, middle, or bottom?

Most B2B teams treat referrals like a nice surprise instead of a channel they run on purpose.

That's backwards. Referrals convert better than almost anything else you'll run, because you're borrowing trust that already exists.

Stop waiting for them to show up. Ask directly. "Do you know anyone else who'd get value from this?" is a real question, not a favor.

Then back it with an incentive. Cash for a closed deal. Account credit. A plan upgrade. Pick whatever fits your product and make it worth their time.

One team I know of built this into their playbook for a specific market. Instead of cold outreach, they went straight to happy customers already in that space and offered a payout per referred contract that closed.

You're not just getting a warm lead. You're outsourcing a slice of your sales team to people who already trust you.

Most teams set targets by guessing at the top of the funnel.

There's a better way, and it starts at the other end.

Start with the revenue number you actually need to hit. Then work backward through every stage between that number and today. Close rate, show rate, meeting rate, all the way up.

That backward math tells you exactly how much volume you need at the very top of the funnel, not a number that feels ambitious.

It also tells you which stage to fix first. If your close rate is weak, more top-of-funnel volume won't save the quarter. Fixing the weak stage will.

Most teams build targets bottom-up instead, starting from current volume and hoping for a reasonable lift. That's a guess wearing a spreadsheet.

Work backward from the finish line, not forward from a guess.

posts.content:
Most B2B emails get opened and immediately ignored.

That's not a subject line problem. It's a voice problem.

I rewrote a webinar reminder last week that had gone out to hundreds of contacts. Tons of opens, almost no clicks.

The fix wasn't cleverer copy. It was less of it.

Three sentences. No bullet points. One link, max.

I opened with something a colleague would actually say. "Hi John, hope you're having a great Wednesday." Then the real ask, low pressure, like I was just checking in.

Subject line went casual too. Something like "will I see you tomorrow?" instead of anything with the word "webinar" in it.

People don't open emails from brands. They open emails from people.

Write every email like you're messaging one specific person, not blasting a list.

Most people's AI copy sounds like AI wrote it.

That's not a model problem. It's a prompting problem.

Start by telling it "make this sound more human, more genuine." Say it again if the first draft still feels stiff.

Cut every em dash. In Claude, you can set "never use em dashes" once in your preferences and it sticks across everything you write from then on.

Kill the bullet points too, at least in emails. They're the fastest way to make a message look like a mail blast instead of a note from a person.

Feed it real examples of copy you actually like before you ask for anything new. AI matches tone way better when it has something to copy from.

Then prompt it directly: "write this like a colleague emailing a colleague, no company voice."

The AI gets you ninety percent there. Your taste closes the gap.

Every junk lead you send back to Meta makes your ads worse.

Meta's algorithm only knows what you tell it. If every signup counts the same in your conversion event, it just finds you more signups.

Not more customers.

The fix is a conversion setup most teams skip. Send qualified leads back as a separate event from junk leads, or assign conversion values so a real opportunity is worth something and a dead lead is worth zero.

Do that and the algorithm stops chasing volume. It starts chasing value, because that's the only signal you gave it.

Works for B2B lead gen, ecommerce, or freemium signups. Whatever event you optimize for is the behavior you get more of.

Stop training your ads to bring you more junk.

One hour of talking becomes a month of content, and none of it feels recycled because it's all coming from the same real conversation.

You can lose money on every new customer and still be right, if the lifetime value math backs it up.

Unless you're sitting on more funding than you know what to do with, every funnel needs to earn its keep. That means looking at the conversion rate at each stage, not just the top-line spend number.

Map it out. Cost to acquire, conversion rate stage by stage, and what a customer is actually worth over their lifetime.

Sometimes taking a loss upfront makes sense, if the lifetime value more than covers it down the line. That's a real strategy, not a red flag.

But if you run the numbers and the lifetime value never catches up to what you're spending, that's your answer. Stop funding that funnel and put the budget somewhere the math actually works.
